facts.fact: Australopithecus, a group of hominins close to modern humans, lived about 4.4 to 1.4 million years ago.
Homo habilis is the earliest member of the genus Homo, living in sub-Saharan Africa 2 to 1.5 million years ago.
The first Homo erectus fossil was discovered on Java Island in 1891.
Homo erectus is called the 'missing link' between apes and humans.
Neanderthal fossils were first discovered in Germany in 1856.
Modern Homo sapiens evolved in Africa about 315,000 years ago.
The oldest modern Homo sapiens sapiens fossils were found at Cro-Magnon in France.
The earliest Homo erectus evidence in India comes from the Narmada valley (Homo erectus narmadensis).
The earliest known human form in India is Homo erectus.
The 'Narmada Man' skull cap was found at Hathnora in the Narmada valley (MP) by Arun Sonakia in 1982.
The Narmada Man fossil belongs to the Middle Pleistocene.
Homo sapiens appear in India roughly 70,000-50,000 years ago, at Jwalapuram (Andhra Pradesh) and Bhimbetka.
No Australopithecus or Neanderthal fossils have been found in India.
The Stone Age is the prehistoric cultural stage defined by the making and use of stone tools.
The Stone Age began with the first hominids and lasted until the development of agriculture.
The three-age archaeological system (Stone-Bronze-Iron) was devised by Christian Jurgensen Thomsen in 1820.
The Stone Age is divided into the Palaeolithic, Mesolithic and Neolithic ages, in that order.
The Palaeolithic Age lasted up to about 10,000 BC.
The Mesolithic Age spans roughly 9000-4000 BC.
In India the Neolithic Age is dated about 4000-1000 BC (Mehrgarh is earlier, c. 7000 BC).
The Chalcolithic Age, which follows the Neolithic and is not one of the three Stone-Age periods, is also called the Copper Age.
The Chalcolithic Age in India is dated about 3500-1000 BC.
The term 'Palaeolithic' was introduced by John Lubbock in 1865.
Palaeolithic people are called 'Quartzite Men' because their tools were of quartzite.
The Palaeolithic corresponds to the Pleistocene epoch (Ice Age), not the Holocene.
Palaeolithic people did not know pottery, agriculture or metals.
The Palaeolithic is the 'Old Stone Age'.
The Palaeolithic is the earliest and longest period of human history.
The Palaeolithic begins about 2.6 million years ago.
The main occupation of Palaeolithic people was hunting and food gathering.
Lower Palaeolithic: up to 100,000 BC; Middle: 100,000-40,000 BC; Upper: 40,000-10,000 BC.
The chronological order is Lower Palaeolithic, Middle Palaeolithic, Upper Palaeolithic, then Mesolithic.
Lower Palaeolithic tools are hand axes, cleavers, choppers and chopping tools.
There is no evidence of burials in the Lower Palaeolithic.
Lower Palaeolithic people built shelters of tree branches, leaves and stones.
The Middle Palaeolithic is dominated by flake tools (scrapers, borers, points).
The Upper Palaeolithic is marked by burins and scrapers.
The Upper Palaeolithic had a developed flint industry.
Modern Homo sapiens emerged in the Upper Palaeolithic.
In the standard view, blade technology (long thin flakes from a prepared core) belongs to the Upper Palaeolithic; the source text lists blades under the Middle phase.
Bone, antler and ivory tools such as needles and harpoons came into wide use in the Upper Palaeolithic.
Sir Alexander Cunningham was the first Director of the Archaeological Survey of India (1861).
Robert Bruce Foote is the 'Father of Indian Pre-history'.
Robert Bruce Foote discovered the Pallavaram Hand Axe.
The Pallavaram hand axe was found in 1863.
Pallavaram is in Tamil Nadu.
V. S. Wakankar discovered the Bhimbetka rock shelters in 1957-58.
The Belan valley (UP/MP) is rich in stone tools and animal fossils of both the Lower and Middle Palaeolithic.
Bhimbetka (MP) is one of the largest prehistoric complexes and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Bhimbetka was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003.
Bhimbetka is in Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh.
The Sohan (Soan) valley Palaeolithic sites lie in West Punjab, Pakistan.
Upper Palaeolithic bone tools in India come only from the Kurnool caves (Andhra Pradesh).
The Kurnool caves are a Palaeolithic site in Andhra Pradesh.
Renugunta is a Palaeolithic site in Andhra Pradesh.
Jwalapuram (Kurnool district) is a Palaeolithic site in Andhra Pradesh.
Attirampakkam is a Palaeolithic site in Tamil Nadu.
The Hunsgi valley is a Palaeolithic site in Karnataka.
Pahalgam is a Palaeolithic site in the Kashmir valley.
Singhbhum is a Palaeolithic site in Jharkhand.
Didwana, Budha Pushkar and Bagor are Palaeolithic sites in Rajasthan.
Nevasa (Maharashtra) gives the Middle Palaeolithic its Indian name, the Nevasan culture.
The Sabarmati valley is an Upper Palaeolithic site in Gujarat.
Jogdaha (Lower Palaeolithic) and Singrauli (Upper Palaeolithic) are sites in Madhya Pradesh.
Patne is a Palaeolithic-Mesolithic site in Maharashtra.
Ostrich eggshell from the Kurnool caves and other sites proves ostriches lived in Palaeolithic India.
The Mesolithic is the transition between the Palaeolithic and the Neolithic.
The Mesolithic belongs to the Holocene, which began after the Pleistocene Ice Age.
Microliths, tiny 1-2 cm tools of flint or chert, are the defining tools of the Mesolithic.
Microliths were mounted on wooden shafts to make spears, harpoons and arrows.
The domestication of animals began in the Mesolithic.
Adamgarh (MP) and Bagor (Rajasthan) give the earliest evidence of animal domestication.
Handmade dull-brown/black pottery began at Sanganakallu (Karnataka) in the Mesolithic.
At Damdama (UP) three human skeletons were found in a single grave.
The Bhimbetka caves hold Mesolithic rock paintings of hunting, food gathering, dancing and daily life.
Mesolithic people moved from nomadic hunting-gathering to herding, and grew a little wheat and barley at the end of the period.
Mesolithic people began living in semi-permanent settlements near rivers and rock shelters.
Mesolithic people wore clothes made of animal skins.
Bagor (Rajasthan), also spelt Baghore, is the largest Mesolithic site in India.
Langhnaj is a Mesolithic site in Gujarat.
Chopani Mando (UP) shows the earliest pottery stage.
Tilwara (Rajasthan) and Kuchai (Odisha) are Mesolithic microlith sites.
Pachmarhi (MP) and Hatkhamba (Maharashtra) are Mesolithic sites.
The cultivation of cereals became established only in the Neolithic.
The Neolithic is the 'New Stone Age'.
The Neolithic marks the shift from hunting-gathering to agriculture and animal husbandry.
Polished stone tools are the hallmark of the Neolithic.
Neolithic people were the first to live in permanent settlements of built houses.
Neolithic crops included wheat, barley, ragi, horse gram and cotton.
Mehrgarh (Balochistan, Pakistan) is the oldest Neolithic site of the subcontinent, c. 7000 BC.
Mehrgarh has the earliest evidence of villages and farming in the subcontinent.
Mehrgarh houses were square or rectangular mud-brick houses.
Mehrgarh (Bolan Pass, Balochistan) is called the 'Bread Basket'.
Mehrgarh yielded einkorn wheat, six-row barley, granaries and bitumen-lined baskets.
Burzahom (Kashmir) is famous for pit-dwellings dug into the ground with steps.
At Burzahom domestic dogs were buried with their masters, showing belief in an afterlife.
Burzahom is in Srinagar district, Kashmir.
Burzahom was first excavated in 1939.
Burzahom is a Neolithic pit-dwelling site, not a site of rock-cut shrines.
Gufkral is a Neolithic site in Kashmir.
Gufkral (Tral, Pulwama) means 'cave of the potter'.
Gufkral shows aceramic Neolithic, ceramic Neolithic and megalithic phases.
Chirand (Bihar) is known for Neolithic bone tools and weapons.
Chechar is a Neolithic site in Bihar.
Neolithic pottery types include grey ware, black-burnished ware and mat-impressed ware.
The wheel and the controlled use of fire are Neolithic milestones.
Neolithic food surplus led to granaries and storage pits.
A celt is a polished stone axe or adze head - a Neolithic tool.
'Celt' comes from Latin celtis, meaning chisel.
Rice was first grown north of the Vindhyas, at Koldihwa and Mahagara in the Belan valley (UP).
Koldihwa is the earliest-rice site in the Belan valley.
Mahagara (Belan valley) had circular huts and a cattle pen.
Lahuradeva (UP) is among the oldest rice sites, about 6400 BCE.
Tokwa is a Belan-valley (UP) site with early evidence of agriculture.
Daojali Hading is a Neolithic site in Assam.
The Garo Hills (Meghalaya) show the development of agriculture in the north-east.
Piklihal is a Neolithic site in Karnataka (Raichur).
Utnur is a Neolithic site in Telangana (Adilabad).
Piklihal and Utnur are Neolithic sites.
An ash mound is a heap of burnt cow-dung marking a Neolithic cattle pen, as at Piklihal and Utnur.
Hallur (Haveri, Karnataka) is known for early iron.
Paiyampalli is a Neolithic site in Tamil Nadu.
Maski (Raichur, Karnataka) is both a Neolithic site and the site of Ashoka's minor rock edict.
Nagarjunakonda is a Neolithic site in present-day Andhra Pradesh.
Tekkalakota, Brahmagiri, Kupgal, Kodekal and Narsipur are Neolithic sites in Karnataka.
Kili Gul Muhammad is a Neolithic site in Balochistan, Pakistan.
Prehistoric art includes cave paintings, rock engravings and miniature figurative carvings.
Prehistoric paintings used ochre and burnt wood on cave walls.
Bhimbetka, the Belan valley and the Narmada valley have art from all three Stone-Age phases.
Prehistoric paintings show humans, animals and geometric patterns, with hunting and family scenes.
Most rock paintings belong to the Upper Palaeolithic, with the highest density in the Mesolithic.
Chalcolithic people began using copper and bronze to make tools.
The Chalcolithic used copper, not iron, which belongs to the later Megalithic/Iron Age.
Chalcolithic cultures lay mainly in the Chhota Nagpur plateau, Upper Gangetic basin, Karnataka and along the Narmada.
Chalcolithic people lived in thatched mud-brick houses and practised Jhum (shifting) cultivation.
Ganeshwar (Rajasthan) is a major copper-artefact site of the Jodhpura culture.
Black and Red Ware (BRW), wheel-made and brightly coloured, is the signature Chalcolithic pottery.
Chalcolithic ornaments were of semi-precious stones: agate, jasper, chalcedony and carnelian.
Chalcolithic crops included green gram, lentil, grass pea, black gram, rice and wheat.
Chalcolithic people kept cows, sheep, goats, pigs and buffaloes and hunted deer.
Chalcolithic copper tools included knives, axes, chisels, rods, pins and fishing hooks.
Fishing was important to riverside Chalcolithic communities, and millets were among their crops.
Large rectangular houses of Chalcolithic village chiefs are early evidence of social inequality.
The Ahar-Banas culture (3000-1500 BC, Rajasthan), adjacent to the IVC, is known for Black and Red Ware.
Ahar is in Rajasthan, near Udaipur.
Lapis lazuli (from Afghanistan) shows the long-distance trade of the Ahar-Banas culture.
Kayatha (2400-2000 BC) is the earliest agricultural settlement of the Malwa region.
Navdatoli is the largest and representative site of the Malwa culture; Eran and Nagda are others.
The Savalda culture (2000-1800 BC) was influenced by Mesolithic cultures of northern Maharashtra and Harappans in Gujarat.
The Jorwe culture (1400-700 BC) had a chalcedony blade-flake industry.
The Prabhas and Rangpur cultures, derived from the Harappans, are known for Lustrous Red Ware.
Rangpur is in Gujarat.
Inamgaon (Maharashtra) is the largest Jorwe Chalcolithic settlement.
Daimabad is a Chalcolithic site in Maharashtra.
Iron artefacts are common at Megalithic sites.
The Megalithic culture introduced tank irrigation in South India.
Megalithic dead were buried in stone boxes called cists.
Megalithic grave goods reflected the social status of the dead.
Megalithic burial pits were marked by four or five posts.
Sangam literature describes South Indian Megalithic burial practices.
Megalithic-type burials persist among the Maria Gonds (Chhattisgarh), Bondos (Odisha) and Khasis.
Adichanallur and Kodumanal are Megalithic sites in Tamil Nadu.
Junapani is a Megalithic site in Maharashtra.
Mangadu (Kerala) is a Megalithic site.
'Megalith' means large stone (mega + lith); megaliths were burials or commemorative memorials.
Dolmens and passage graves are Megalithic tomb types.
Burial urns belong mainly to the Chalcolithic/Bronze Age.
Chandraketugarh is in West Bengal (not Odisha) and is famous for terracotta art.
Atranjikhera, an Ochre Coloured Pottery (OCP) site, is in Uttar Pradesh (not Rajasthan).
Salihundam (Andhra Pradesh) is a Buddhist stupa site, not a rock-cut site.
Bairat (Rajasthan) has Buddhist (Ashokan) remains.
'Halbi, Ho and Kui' are tribal languages, not archaeological cultures.
Celt = Neolithic, microlith = Mesolithic, burin = Upper Palaeolithic, cleaver = Lower Palaeolithic.
A burin is a chisel-like tool for engraving bone, antler and wood.
Core tools (hand-axe, cleaver) are Lower Palaeolithic; flake tools are Middle Palaeolithic.
The Levallois technique (prepared core struck for planned flakes) is Middle Palaeolithic.
Mousterian is the world term for the Middle Palaeolithic flake-tool culture.
The Nevasan culture is the Indian name for the Middle Palaeolithic.
The Acheulean and Soanian traditions belong to the Lower Palaeolithic.
Oldowan is the earliest pebble/chopping-tool industry.
In the Middle Palaeolithic, quartzite gave way to chert, jasper and agate.
